notes.claim: The mains supply in the UK is alternating current at 50 hertz and 230 volts; UK regulations declare a low voltage supply as 50 hertz and 230 volts between phase and neutral, unless otherwise agreed.
Impedance, like resistance, is measured in ohms.
Engineers write j for the square root of minus one because i already stands for electric current.
Adding a capacitor in parallel with a lagging inductive load draws a leading current that partly or completely neutralises the load’s lagging reactive current, so the supply current falls.
Multiplying a number by minus one turns its arrow through 180 degrees, a half turn.
Multiplying a real or complex number by j rotates it by plus 90 degrees, and j squared is minus one.
Engineers use the symbol j for this number because i is already used for current.
The same number is written i in maths and j in electrical engineering.

Introducing j as the square root of minus one is contested: mathcentre starts from j = √−1 and gets j² = −1 from it, while one paper on teaching calls that start unjustifiable because it leads to misconceptions.
notes.contested: mathcentre defines j as √−1 and derives j² = −1; the Scimath teaching paper argues against defining it as √−1.

notes.claim: A complex number is drawn on a plane with a horizontal real axis and a vertical imaginary axis.
Adding complex numbers is essentially the same as adding two-dimensional vectors.
Addition is most easily done in Cartesian form, multiplication and division in polar form, so you choose the form that suits the sum.
On the complex plane, an impedance on the real axis such as 6 + j0 is a pure resistance, and one on the j axis such as 0 + j4 a pure reactance.
Multiplying complex numbers in rectangular form follows the rules of normal algebra, with j squared put equal to minus one.
Multiplying two complex numbers multiplies their moduli and adds their arguments.
Multiplying by j alone is a pure turn of plus 90 degrees.
The conjugate of a + bi is a - bi: the same number with the sign of the imaginary part changed.
On the plane the conjugate is the mirror image of the number in the real axis.
A complex number times its conjugate is a real number.
Division is done by multiplying numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate of the denominator.
The modulus is the distance of the point (a, b) from the origin, and it is never negative.
The argument is the angle between the positive real axis and the line from the origin to the point.
A complex number with modulus r and argument theta is written r angle theta.
When finding the angle with an inverse tangent, check the quadrant, because a calculator’s answer may not be in the correct one.
Going back from length and angle: the across part is r cos theta and the up part is r sin theta.

The argument is normally taken in the interval minus pi (not included) to pi, that is more than −180° and up to 180°, though adding any whole number of turns gives the same direction; HN units call this the principal argument.
A phasor is a complex number that represents the magnitude and phase of a voltage or a current; the marine syllabus resolves phasors into their two components.
In polar form, to multiply you multiply the moduli and add the arguments.
To divide in polar form, you divide the moduli and subtract the arguments.
Multiplication and division are most easily done in polar form, while addition and subtraction are easier in Cartesian form.
A complex number r∠θ can also be written in exponential form re^(jθ), with θ in radians.
Impedance is measured in ohms and is the AC analogue of resistance, combining the effects of resistance, capacitive reactance and inductive reactance.
On the impedance plane, resistance points right, inductive impedance (90 degrees) points up and capacitive impedance (minus 90 degrees) points down.
Inductive reactance is X_L = 2 pi f L when frequency f is in hertz, and capacitive reactance is X_C = 1/(omega C).
The peak current in an inductor is proportional to the angular frequency, while a capacitor’s reactance tends to zero at very high frequencies.
A secondary source (Kirtley's power-systems text) notes that the phase angle between voltage and current is the same as the phase angle of the impedance.
Most ships at sea run at 60 Hz.
Ohm’s law is applied in AC circuits with impedance: current is voltage divided by impedance, I = E/Z.
Impedances add in series, and their reciprocals add in parallel, just as resistances do.
One university course says all the DC circuit analysis techniques work with AC if you handle the complex arithmetic.
The phase angle between voltage and current is the same as the phase angle of the impedance.
In a parallel AC circuit the branch currents add to form the total current, as in DC.
A capacitor in parallel with an inductive load draws a leading current that cancels part or all of the load’s lagging reactive current, lowering the supply current.
